title: Doppler Effect in Sound and Light
short_intro: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency of a wave received by an observer due to relative motion between the source and the observer. It applies to both longitudinal waves (such as sound in a medium) and transverse waves (such as light in a vacuum).

exam_scope.tgt_core: Apparent frequency formulas for a moving source and/or moving observer in a stationary medium; reflections from moving walls; basic numerical problem-solving.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: General relative motion at an arbitrary angle, relativistic Doppler effect for light, longitudinal and transverse Doppler effect, and astrophysical applications.

prerequisites: Wave motion and wave equation kinematics
Relationship between frequency, wavelength, and wave velocity

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental Mechanism of Doppler Shift
bullets: When a source moves toward an observer, successive wave crests are emitted closer together, effectively reducing the observed wavelength.
When an observer moves toward a source, the rate of intercepting wave fronts increases, leading to a higher observed frequency.
The medium provides a fixed frame of reference for sound waves, meaning the speed of sound depends on the motion of the observer and source relative to the medium.

concept_notes.heading: Asymmetry in Sound Doppler Effect
bullets: The apparent frequency depends on whether the source is moving or the observer is moving, even if the relative speed between them is identical.
For a stationary observer and moving source, the wavelength changes in the medium.
For a moving observer and stationary source, the wavelength in the medium remains unchanged, but the relative speed of wave interception changes.

concept_notes.heading: Reflections and Echoes
bullets: When a sound wave reflects from a moving wall or obstacle, the wall acts first as a moving observer and then as a moving source.
The beat frequency heard when combining the direct and reflected sound is frequently tested in examinations.
Doppler radar utilizes this principle to measure the speed of moving vehicles or meteorological formations.

concept_notes.heading: Relativistic Doppler Effect for Light
bullets: Light waves require no material medium; thus, only the relative velocity between source and observer matters.
Longitudinal relativistic Doppler shift accounts for both time dilation and the classical frequency shift.
Transverse Doppler effect is purely a relativistic phenomenon arising entirely from time dilation.

derivations.title: General Formula for Sound Doppler Effect
derivations.conditions: Source and observer moving along the line joining them in a stationary medium
steps: Let v be the speed of sound, v_s be the speed of the source, and v_o be tobacco/observer speed. Let f be the source frequency.
If the source moves toward a stationary observer at speed v_s, the effective wavelength becomes lambda' = (v - v_s) / f.
The observed frequency is f' = v / lambda' = v / [(v - v_s) / f] = f (v / (v - v_s)).
If the observer also moves toward the source at speed v_o, the relative velocity of waves with respect to the observer is v + v_o.
Combining both motions yields the general expression: f' = f *  rac{v pm v_o}{v mp v_s}.
derivations.result: f' = f *  rac{v pm v_o}{v mp v_s}

derivations.title: Relativistic Longitudinal Doppler Effect for Light
derivations.conditions: Source and observer moving directly toward or away from each other in free space
steps: Consider a source emitting light of frequency f in its proper frame. In the observer's frame, time dilation stretches the period by a factor of gamma.
Account for the propagation delay as the source moves closer or further away during emission of successive cycles.
Combine the Doppler factor with the Lorentz transformation factor sqrt( rac{1 -  eta}{1 +  eta}), where  eta = v / c.
For a source approaching the observer: f' = f sqrt{ rac{1 +  eta}{1 -  eta}}.
derivations.result: f' = f sqrt{ rac{1 +  eta}{1 -  eta}}

formula_sheet.name: General Doppler Frequency (Sound)
formula_sheet.variables: f' = apparent frequency, f = true frequency, v = speed of sound, v_o = observer speed, v_s = source speed
formula_sheet.conditions: Speeds must be less than the speed of sound; upper signs for approaching, lower for receding.

formula_sheet.name: Source Moving, Observer Stationary
formula_sheet.variables: v_s = source speed (+ when moving away, - when moving toward)
formula_sheet.conditions: Observer at rest relative to the medium.

formula_sheet.name: Observer Moving, Source Stationary
formula_sheet.variables: v_o = observer speed (+ when moving toward, - when moving away)
formula_sheet.conditions: Source at rest relative to the medium.

formula_sheet.name: Apparent Wavelength from Moving Source
formula_sheet.conditions: Source moving towards (-) or away from (+) the point of observation.

formula_sheet.name: Beat Frequency from Reflection off Moving Wall
formula_sheet.variables: f_b = beat frequency, v_s = speed of wall

formula_sheet.name: Relativistic Longitudinal Doppler Effect (Light)
formula_sheet.variables: \beta = v / c (ratio of relative velocity to speed of light)

formula_sheet.name: Transverse Doppler Effect
formula_sheet.conditions: Motion is perpendicular to the line of sight at the point of closest approach.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Frequency vs. Time for a Moving Train (Whistle)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A discontinuous drop in observed frequency f' as a train passes an observer, plotted against time t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As the train approaches, f' is constant and higher than f. At the instant of crossing, there is an abrupt step-down to a constant lower frequency as it recedes.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification of the frequency curve and calculation of train speed from frequency limits.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wavefront Compression Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Concentric circles crowding together in front of a moving sound source and spreading out behind it.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates asymmetric wavelength variation in the propagation medium due to source kinematics.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions explaining why wavelength changes ahead of a moving source.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Astrological Redshift vs. Blueshift Spectral Lines
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Emission/absorption spectra shifted toward the red (longer wavelength) or blue (shorter wavelength) end relative to a laboratory reference spectrum.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Redshift indicates recession (expanding universe); blueshift indicates approach.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Calculations involving stellar radial velocities using fractional wavelength shifts.

solved_numericals.question: A source of sound emitting a frequency of 500 Hz moves toward a stationary observer with a velocity of 30 m/s. If the velocity of sound in air is 330 m/s, calculate the apparent frequency heard by the observer.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: f = 500 Hz, v_s = 30 m/s, v_o = 0, v = 330 m/s.
Select the appropriate formula for a moving source and stationary observer: f' = f * [v / (v - v_s)].

solved_numericals.question: An observer is moving with a velocity of 20 m/s toward a stationary source emitting sound of frequency 400 Hz. What is the apparent frequency heard? (Speed of sound = 340 m/s).
solution_steps: Identify parameters: f = 400 Hz, v_o = 20 m/s (moving toward), v_s = 0, v = 340 m/s.
Use formula for moving observer: f' = f * [(v + v_o) / v].

solved_numericals.question: A star is moving away from the Earth with a speed of 3.0 * 10^6 m/s. What is the fractional change in the wavelength of a spectral line observed from the star? (Speed of light c = 3.0 * 10^8 m/s).
solution_steps: Identify parameters: v = 3.0 * 10^6 m/s, c = 3.0 * 10^8 m/s.
Use the Doppler formula for light at low velocities: Delta_lambda / lambda = v / c.

assumptions_and_limitations: The medium is assumed to be uniform, homogeneous, and stationary unless wind velocity is explicitly factored in.
The speeds of the source and observer must be less than the wave propagation speed in the medium (v_s < v) to avoid shock wave formation (Mach cone).
Classical acoustic Doppler formulas do not account for relativistic effects, which become necessary only at extreme astrophysical velocities.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The apparent frequency depends only on the relative speed between the source and observer.
common_misconceptions.correct: For sound waves, the apparent frequency depends separately on the individual velocities of the source and observer relative to the medium.
common_misconceptions.why: The medium establishes a preferred reference frame for acoustic waves, violating simple Galilean velocity addition symmetry.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At the exact instant the source passes the observer, the observed frequency equals the true frequency.
common_misconceptions.correct: The observed frequency experiences an abrupt drop at the crossing point because the component of velocity along the line of sight changes sign instantaneously.
common_misconceptions.why: Finite propagation delay and transverse velocity components dictate that the transition is discontinuous in idealized models.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Light experiences the same Doppler formula as sound because both are wave phenomena.
common_misconceptions.correct: Light requires no medium and is governed by relativistic kinematics, resulting in a different mathematical formula.
common_misconceptions.why: Electromagnetic waves obey the theory of special relativity, incorporating time dilation and Lorentz contraction.

quick_revision: Apparent frequency increases when source/observer approach each other and decreases when they recede.
A moving source alters the wavelength in the medium, whereas a moving observer alters the rate of wave interception.
The relativistic transverse Doppler effect is a purely kinematic consequence of time dilation with no classical acoustic analog.
